runs.analysis:
Candidate A stays close to the source files. It uses the Builder's Foundation path, the 14 km Tarifa–Tangier span, the €4-6B contingency, the €200-500M marine fund, the €3-8B maintenance trust and the €2-4B decommissioning reserve. It also uses the November 2026 ministerial meeting, the 8,000-12,000 workforce and the 2046 target. Its risk section covers the main plan risks with specific mitigations. It has flaws:
- It says "five dimensions" but lists six.
- It claims geotechnical studies are "already commissioned", which the plan does not say.
- It uses overclaiming rhetoric such as "engineers certainty" and a "200-year legacy".
- It gives no revenue or demand numbers.
These are minor next to B's problems.

Candidate B is longer and more structured, and its call to action and collaboration sections are more actionable. Its risk section is also richer, with 11 risks carrying impact figures drawn from the plan. However, it invents many unsupported figures and facts:
- €200B+ in trade flows and a €500B multiplier.
- Fare revenue of €15-25B and tolls of €5-10B, even though the project has no road component.
- Spain–Morocco trade of €5B in 2024 growing 12% a year.
- Paris–Casablanca travel time falling from 18 to 4 hours.
- A "$3-5B" first tranche.
- BNDES as a financing partner.
- Bering Strait ambitions.

It also contradicts the inputs:
- It says the Azores-Gibraltar fault zone "is mapped and understood", while the plan flags a complete absence of a site-specific seismic assessment.
- It puts the Channel Tunnel depth at 37.9m, when the source gives about 75m.
- It claims the 73% Channel Tunnel overrun "won't repeat—we've priced it in".
- It says "in less than 15 minutes", which does not match the 14 km span.
- It asks for treaty ratification in "30 days".
- It sets an unsupported mobilization date of September 2028.

These fabrications and overclaims would mislead downstream stages and stakeholders. A is the more faithful and internally consistent output.

Candidate A is far more specific and decision-useful. It has a concrete 30-day call to action with dated gates, 11 risks with impacts and mitigations drawn from project_plan.md, measurable success metrics, tailored stakeholder benefits, and collaboration tracks with timelines and a financing tranche structure. It also uses the Channel Tunnel, Seikan and Marmaray precedents from similar_projects.md. Its weaknesses are real. It invents figures not in the inputs: €200B+ trade flows, €15-25B fare revenue, a Spain-Morocco trade figure of €5B (likely understated), and an 18h-to-4h travel claim. It mixes currencies ("$3-5B" next to euro figures). Some numbers conflict, for example a €50B NPV against roughly €20-35B of total revenue. It lists a "Sept 2027" milestone that clashes with its own 18-month ratification window. The long_term_vision is also bloated and repetitive. Candidate B is faithful, concise and consistent with the inputs, but it is generic. Its risk section covers only about five risks, and its call to action is vague ("Visit our project portal"). It says "five dimensions" but lists six. It also makes unsupported claims such as "every risk has a named owner" and "engineers certainty". It has little quantification and no real use of the precedent projects. Overall, A's depth and actionability outweigh its hallucinated numbers, though those are a notable flaw.

Candidate A is compact and tied to the source files. It names the Pragmatic Scale-Up path, the 60% take-or-pay gate, the binding RTE allocation before FID, the 75% local hiring rule, and the decision numbers. It keeps the skeptical, gated framing the plan requires. It has flaws. The 25% ecological offset sits awkwardly beside the 80% buffer, and the "Q4 2026 Phase 1 FID" is unrealistic given a one-year Phase 0. Its opening is also somewhat hype-y. Even so, it invents little and it covers every schema field.

Candidate B is far longer and reads as promotional copy that contradicts the plan's red-team, skeptical brief. It invents many unsupported facts. These include 5,000+ and 25,000+ jobs, 4+ GW of heat reuse, "cash-positive within 3 years", a Phase 1 FID in Q2 2027, and PIG status by Q2 2027. It also reserves "2 GW+ for classified workloads", names Anthropic and Tesla as tenants, and claims "no alternative site in Europe" and "proven mitigation". It leaves a "$X per-megawatt" placeholder. It treats 161 km² as assembled and moats the project, although the plan says that land may be infeasible. It ignores the plan's insistence that external approvals be treated as uncertain. Its call to action asks DGSI and RTE to commit to fast-track reviews, and it has timeline inconsistencies. Some mitigations are specific and useful, but the length and the fabrication make it less faithful and less useful downstream.

A is better on faithfulness and consistency with the skeptical premise.

Candidate A fills every schema field with substantial, plan-specific content. It has audience-segmented calls to action, seven concrete risks with mitigations tied to the plan's own gates (RTE, DGSI, 60% take-or-pay, holding costs, PUE), and detailed metrics, stakeholder benefits and collaboration. Its weaknesses are invented figures (5,000 and 25,000 jobs, 4 GW heat reuse, 2 GW+ classified), overreaching claims, inconsistent land percentages (25% vs 80%), a Q2 2027 FID that conflicts with its own pre-FID conditions, and a promotional tone at odds with the skeptical brief. Candidate B stays more faithful to the inputs and cites decisions correctly, but it is very thin. Its audience is one line, it covers only three risks, and its metrics and vision are minimal and generic. Its call to action demands commitments within 90 days to hit a Q4 2026 construction FID, which is unrealistic against the plan's Phase 0 and its binding RTE gate. Its hype tone is also off. A is more useful despite its flaws.

Candidate A is far more complete and plan-specific. It fills every schema field in depth and ties its content to the upstream files: the Builder scenario, the Three Strikes policy, the €300M Emergency Float Reserve, the 150% coverage threshold, the 65% emergency consensus, PRM conformance at month 18, the 90-minute threshold and the 90% uptime incentive. Its call to action is segmented by audience. Its risk section has five categories, each with a risk and a mitigation. Its metrics, stakeholder benefits and collaboration sections are specific and useful downstream.

A also has real flaws. The pitch says "40% of cross-border passengers choose flying", which misuses the 40% target. It invents figures with no basis in the inputs: 15-25% revenue uplift, a €5-10B market, a 45-day to <10-day complaint resolution time, and "rail 45-50% share". It names bodies the inputs don't mention, such as an "EU Accessibility Enforcement Body" and "urban air mobility". It carries over the odd "Decision 25/14" reference, and "Displacing 40%+ of short-haul flights" is inconsistent with the rest. The "Q2 2026 sandbox" is dubious. It is also verbose.

Candidate B is concise, faithful and consistent with the inputs. However, it is thin. The target audience is one line. The risks section covers only two risks. The metrics are sparse and omit the complaint-halving and modal-shift targets. Collaboration, stakeholder benefits and ethics are brief and generic. The long-term vision is short, and its claim that "bus/ferry pilots underway" contradicts the plan's deferral of non-rail modes. Its "18-month standardization rush" sits awkwardly with the realistic framing. It has little hallucination, but it offers much less decision-useful content.

Overall, A's depth and specificity outweigh its invented numbers.

Candidate A is concise and mostly faithful to the source documents, but it is thin. The pitch omits the €1.5B budget, the four corridors and accessibility. The metrics leave out the 50% complaint reduction and the modal-shift measure. The call to action is vague, and it invents a few claims such as "bus/ferry pilots underway".

Candidate B is much more complete and decision-useful. It gives audience-specific calls to action, categorized risks with mitigations drawn from the plan (the €300M reserve, the 150% coverage trigger, the 65% emergency consensus rule, PRM conformance at month 18, Three Strikes pre-approval), and rich metrics and stakeholder benefits.

B has real flaws. It misstates the 40% target as "40% of passengers choose flying". It also invents statistics (15–25% revenue uplift, a €5–10B market, 45–50% rail share, a 45-to-10-day complaint resolution time), adds a Vienna-Prague corridor, and sets an implausible Q2 2026 sandbox date. It is also verbose.

Overall, B's depth and plan-grounded mitigation edge out A's accuracy-but-sparseness, despite B's hallucinated figures.

Candidate A is the stronger pitch. It is specific to Leipzig and uses the plan's facts: the €300k reserve, 5,000 kits, the 10 May threshold finalization, the Month 2 and Month 4 gates, and the Brussels, Paris and Frankfurt precedents. Its call to action is concrete, its risk table covers the plan's real risks, and its stakeholder, ethics and collaboration sections are thorough. Weaknesses: it is very long, invents some targets (40% Month 2 registry enrollment, ≤105% of baseline EMS calls, a ≥€1.5M Year-2 commitment), and states the 80% gate as "utilization" where the prompt says planned hours delivered. Candidate B is brief and has a hook, but several fields are thin. It contains a clear factual error: "release of the full €3.5M budget tranche", when only €1.5M is gated at Month 4. It also overpromises ("guarantee safety", "100% adherence"), omits the transport-time and after-action gate criteria, and gives shallow risk and metrics content. A is more decision-useful and more useful downstream.

Candidate A is concise and on-theme, but it has several faults. It says the project will "guarantee" safety, which is an overpromise. It says the Month 4 gate secures "the full €3.5M budget tranche", when only €1.5M is released at that point. It uses an odd name, "Leipzig Builder Initiative", and the phrases "triage script bypass" and "premium-priced local procurement" are awkward. Its risk section is thin, with three risks. Its metrics are weak and include an unrealistic "100% adherence". Its stakeholder, ethics, and vision sections are short. Its call to action is concrete, though: sign-off on thresholds by May 10 and release of procurement.

Candidate B is much more complete and decision-useful. It has a clear problem-solution pitch and a detailed, actionable call to action with timings: a 90-minute briefing, the MCR segregation, legal review, canvassing in week 1, and purchase orders in weeks 1-2. Its risk table covers the plan's main risks with likelihood, impact, and mitigation. Those include GDPR, outreach safety, supply chain, alert fatigue, script reliability, and center compliance. Its metrics are staged by gate and include health outcomes, equity, and financial measures. Its stakeholder, ethics, collaboration, and vision sections are specific to the plan. B has flaws too. It implies the Month 2 gate unlocks the second tranche, when Month 4 does. It invents some targets, such as 40% enrollment and ≤105% of baseline EMS calls. Its vision is verbose and grandiose. These flaws are smaller than A's tranche error and thinness, and B better serves downstream stages.
